description: A small Node project that serves one route, and an explicit user goal asking for something it does not have. The project is not defective: what it does, it does. The gap is between the request and the code, and the question the fixture answers is how far SURE is allowed to go in saying so — one candidate, at the weakest level the gravity rule allows, filed as style noise rather than as a blocker.

required_outcomes.why: The acceptance sentence is *explicit intent mismatch can yield grounded finding*, and what this outcome records is how far that reaches today, by equality rather than by paraphrase. One requirement was checked and exactly one came back unmatched; `limitation` is `None`, which is what separates this fixture from `missing-user-intent` — SURE had a request and compared against it. The one proposal is `Severity::Note`, non-critical and `EvidenceClass::Inference`, which `false_completion_aggregator`'s `is_style_noise` rule files in `style_noise()`, so the report shows it in the noise bucket while `material()` is empty. Both buckets are asserted, because `style_noise == 1` alone would be satisfied by a proposal that also appeared in `material()`. The title, the identifier and the sentence a reader is shown are compared whole: the identifier is `check_id("goal", "intentunmatched")`, so a change to how a requirement is named changes it and this test goes red. `not_checked` is asserted at one because the plan surfaces the proposal as a check that could not run, and the last line of the summary is that count — a sentence a reader sees and would otherwise take on the product's word.

required_outcomes.title: the same proposal cannot reach must_fix, because its evidence class cannot support it
required_outcomes.why: This is the half that says *why* the level above is what it is rather than merely that it is. `supports_severity` returns true for every source when the severity does not block hand-off, so a `note` is grounded the moment it has one evidence item — and `Severity::MustFix` is the only severity that blocks hand-off, so `AssessmentSource::Inference` cannot carry it. The rule is asserted as a fact of the source rather than read off this proposal, and the proposal's own class is asserted equal to it, so a change that promoted the proposal's severity would fail here as well as above. Raising it would make every requirement SURE failed to keyword-match a hand-off blocker, and `evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json` asks for `note` on the case this comparison belongs to.

required_outcomes.why: The control the fixture cannot do without. A reporter that called every stated requirement unimplemented would satisfy the outcome above; with the file present the answer must flip — one requirement matched, nothing unmatched, no proposal at all, and the rendered summary losing exactly the `1 check(s) could not run or were skipped.` line and gaining nothing. The file is added to a copy of the fixture's own two sources rather than to a project written out here, and the test asserts that copy differs from the fixture by that one path before it reads either answer.

forbidden_outcomes.description: SURE stays silent about a requirement the user stated and nothing implements. The goal is a fact of the session, not a hint: a report that shows the capability line and `No open findings.` while saying nothing about the requested CSV export leaves the reader to conclude the request was met.

The project is reported as ready to hand off, as passing, or as verified against the request. Nothing in this directory implements the export — no route, no command, no file — so any of those words is a green light on work that is not there.

The mismatch is raised above the level the gravity rule allows: `must_fix`, `critical = true`, a `Finding` that says the project is wrong, or a hand-off blocker. The anchor is the requirement's own identifier, which is not a file a reader can open, and the statement is about SURE's reading rather than about the project. `evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json` asks for `note` on this case, and a wrong blocker is as serious here as a false green. This sentence used to read 'a `Finding` rather than a candidate', and `P7-T012` made that half false: the run now raises exactly one `Finding`, because the requirement's proposal is surfaced as a planned check, this build runs no planned check, and `sure_core::findings_from_checks` raises a `cannot_confirm` finding for a check that reported nothing. What the rule is about is unchanged and the mutation is what separates them: the mismatch itself is never raised — it stays a candidate at `Severity::Note`, `critical == false`, filed as style noise and absent from `material()` — and the finding the run does raise is at that same `note`, its status is `cannot_confirm`, and what it says is that SURE planned a check and did not run it. A build that turned the mismatch into a `must_fix`, a blocker or a defect claim about the project is what this forbids, and that is what `aggregate_material`, `finding_critical` and the ceiling outcome beside it are asserted for.
The project is reported as broken, or its `/invoices` route as a defect. The route is implemented and declared; what is missing is the thing the user asked for, and the two must not be conflated.

notes: There is no case for this fixture in `evaluation/acceptance-manifest.json` — and as of `P14-T010` there is no id that contract names without a directory under `fixtures/adversarial/`. This sentence used to name `benign-test-mocks` as the last one: `P14-T010` wrote that fixture's directory and its project, so the clause shrank to nothing rather than being rewritten, and the id it named was never an intent mismatch either way. That list has shrunk rather than always read this way: when this sentence was written the five ids with no directory were `missing-user-intent`, `benign-test-mocks`, `dynamic-not-authorized`, `force-push` and `sensitive-read`; `P14-T005` through `P14-T008` created the other four directories, none of which is an intent mismatch either, and `P14-T010` created the fifth. It is named in `FIXTURES_WITHOUT_A_MANIFEST_CASE` in `crates/sure-testkit/tests/fixture_apps.rs` with the nearest row and the reason it is a different defect; `every_fixture_without_a_manifest_case_is_one_named_here` checks that claim against the manifest rather than trusting it. `expected_severity` and `release_blocking` are therefore the level the product actually reaches rather than a row copied from the contract, and they agree with `missing-user-intent`'s row because both cases are the same kind of statement: SURE reporting on its own reading of a request. SURE produces exactly one `Finding` for this case since `P7-T012`, and this sentence is where that is written down: the requirement's proposal is surfaced as a planned check, no planned check runs in this build, and `sure_core::findings_from_checks` turns that into one open `cannot_confirm` finding at `Severity::Note` — the proposal's own weight, taken and not chosen. This sentence used to say SURE produced no `Finding` for this case at all, which that change made false. What the fixture pins about the mismatch itself is unchanged: one note, style noise and not material, and a ceiling that cannot be raised through an `Inference` source. The pipeline is driven with `store: None`, so grading this fixture writes nothing anywhere, and the project is read where it ships rather than copied, so a fixture edited without the test being edited is a red test.
